newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Dollar rallies on yen, French shares slide.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Dollar rallies on yen, French shares slide.

text.p: The dollar staged a strong rally against the yen on Thursday though it flagged after its initial big rise, while French shares slipped as investors were prompted by political fears to bank some profits.

The dollar bowed out of European trading off its highs but holding the bulk of the day's gains against the yen after an ebullient response to verbal intervention from officials on both sides of the Pacific.

Japan's finance ministry came out in support of the Bank of Japan's low interest-rate policy, while the BOJ said the yen's correction of its weakness was too rapid. U.S. Trade Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated the U.S. strong dollar policy.
"It's clear from the comments of Japanese officials that they want to stabilise the yen," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International in London.

The dollar charged higher to stand near to 116 yen in early European trade, more than two yen up from late Wednesday. It then wavered back but managed to finish just under 116 yen compared with 113.65 late on Wednesday.
The Japanese government has been battling to give the dollar a leg-up after it sank to five-month lows of 111.88 yen on Tuesday on expectations that Japan may soon raise interest rates.

The dollar also got a lift today from the Swiss National Bank's decision to leave official interest rates unchanged. The dollar stood at 1.4114 Swiss francs in late trade versus 1.4060 late on Wednesday.
That helped support the dollar against the German mark, which firmed a touch to 1.6940 from 1.6918 on Wednesday.
The dollar wobbled against the mark earlier, however, after new data generated optimism over Germany's economic outlook and the Bundesbank dampened speculation of monetary easing there.
French shares closed 1.6 percent lower on profit-taking on the eve of the end of the trading account after recent highs for the blue-chip index, dealers said.
They added that rumours about unpublished opinion polls concerning the May 25 and June 1 two-round parliamentary election were also weighing on the market.
The French share market is expected to slip further on Friday when the May account closes and ahead of the weekend's first round of voting. The CAC-40 closed 44.70 points lower at 2,741.65.
London shares closed moderately higher but a weaker Wall Street took the shine off a promising advance.
The FTSE 100, which raced to an intraday trading high of 4,661.7, a mere 32 points below its record closing peak, finished just 9.8 points firmer to 4,651.8.

"The market chalked up another gain but it wasn't all that convincing," the head of sales and trading at a large brokerage said. "People are worried the Dow might be heading for a correction and don't want to be too aggressive."

Weak bond markets also unsettled investors on both sides of the Atlantic. The yield on the benchmark U.S. 30-year long bond touched the key 7.00 percent level for the first time in nearly two months. A yield above 7.00 percent is usually a bearish sign as investors are more inclined to switch out of shares and into bonds.

In addition, talk of higher interest rates swirled around London dealing rooms after news that April retail sales had risen a monthly 0.1 percent and yearly 4.7 percent against expectations of a monthly 0.3 percent and a yearly 4.1 percent.

"Although April retail sales were on the soft side of expectations, revisions have boosted annual growth to a very robust 4.7 pct. This should be seen as increasing the likelihood that the Bank of England will hike rates soon unless the budget is very tight," said Bank of America's Jeremy Hawkins.
Britain's new Labour Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown is expected to unveil his first budget in the next few weeks.

Dealers said most participants had discounted higher UK interest rates and were now concentrating on how Wall Street performed over the coming weeks. The Dow Industrial Average was down around 25 points by the close of London trade.
German shares gave up early gains and ended lower after being hurt by weakness in German debt markets which capped the advance and prompted the share market sell-off, traders said.
"The losses are due to the debt market," said one trader. "It's hard to understand why both markets are falling."

Bund market traders said squabbling over plans to plug the expected 1997 deficit hole was giving both international and domestic investors an uncomfortable feeling about the German market since no clear strategy had emerged.

The losses came despite a report by the Ifo economic research institute that fuelled hopes of stronger German growth without inflation. The institute's April west German business climate index rose to 94.07 from 92.6 in March.
CLOSING STOCK PRICES
London's FTSE 100 was up 9.8 points at 4,651.8.
The Paris CAC-40 index was down 44.70 points at 2,741.65.
Frankfurt's DAX index ended down 16.67 at 3,579.42. The Ibis DAD of electronic trading was down 24.96 at 3,575.44.
CURRENCIES AT 1600 GMT
The dollar stood at 1.6937 marks and 115.98 yen compared with 1.6918 marks and 113.65 yen in late European trade on Wednesday.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold closed at $342.75 an ounce compared with $342.65 an ounce at Wednesday's close in London.
